vsm2.14:1.1: Now, concentration was described under the heading of consciousness in the stanza:
vsm2.14:1.2: "When a wise man, established well in virtue, / Develops consciousness and understanding (I.1)."
vsm2.14:1.3:
And that has been developed in all its aspects by the bhikkhu who is thus possessed of the more advanced
development of concentration that has acquired with direct-knowledge the benefits described in Chs. XII and XIII.
vsm2.14:1.4: But understanding comes next and that has still to be developed.
vsm2.14:1.5: Now, that is not easy, firstly even to know about, let alone to develop, when it is taught very briefly.
vsm2.14:1.6: In order, therefore, to deal with the detailed method of its development there is the following set of questions:
vsm2.14:1.8: (ii) In what sense is it understanding?
vsm2.14:1.9: (iii) What are its characteristic, function, manifestation, and proximate cause?
vsm2.14:1.10: (iv) How many kinds of understanding are there?
vsm2.14:1.12: (vi) What are the benefits of developing understanding?
vsm2.14:2.3: Understanding (paññā) is of many sorts and has various aspects.
vsm2.14:2.4:
An answer that attempted to explain it all would accomplish neither its intention
nor its purpose, and would, besides, lead to distraction;
vsm2.14:2.5: so we shall confine ourselves to the kind intended here,
vsm2.14:2.6: which is understanding consisting in insight knowledge associated with profitable consciousness.
vsm2.14:3.1: (ii) IN WHAT SENSE IS IT UNDERSTANDING?
vsm2.14:3.2: It is understanding (paññā) in the sense of act of understanding (pajānana).
vsm2.14:3.3: What is this act of understanding?
vsm2.14:3.4: It is knowing (jānana) in a particular mode separate from the modes of perceiving (sañjānana) and cognizing (vijānana).
vsm2.14:3.5:
For though the state of knowing (jānana-bhāva) is equally present in perception (saññā), in consciousness
(viññāṇa), and in understanding (paññā), nevertheless perception is only the mere perceiving of an object as, say, blue or yellow;
vsm2.14:3.6: it cannot bring about the penetration of its characteristics as impermanent, painful, and not-self.
vsm2.14:3.7: Consciousness knows the objects as blue or yellow, and it brings about the penetration of its characteristics,
vsm2.14:3.8: but it cannot bring about, by endeavouring, the manifestation of the supramundane path.
vsm2.14:3.9:
Understanding knows the object in the way already stated, it brings about the penetration of the characteristics, and it
brings about, by endeavouring, the manifestation of the path.
vsm2.14:4.1:
Suppose there were three people, a child without discretion, a villager, and a money-changer,
who saw a heap of coins lying on a money-changer's counter.
vsm2.14:4.2:
The child without discretion knows merely that the coins are figured and ornamented, long, square or round;
he does not know that they are reckoned as valuable for human use and enjoyment.
vsm2.14:4.3:
And the villager knows that they are figured and ornamented, etc., and that they
are reckoned as valuable for human use and enjoyment;
vsm2.14:4.4: but he does not know such distinctions as, "This one is genuine, this is false, this is half-value."
vsm2.14:4.5:
The money-changer knows all those kinds, and he does so by looking at the coin, and by listening to the sound of it
when struck, and by smelling its smell, tasting its taste, and weighing it in his hand, and he knows that it
was made in a certain village or town or city or on a certain mountain or by a certain master.
vsm2.14:4.6: And this may be understood as an illustration.
vsm2.14:5.1:
Perception is like the child without discretion seeing the coin, because it apprehends
the mere mode of appearance of the object as blue and so on.
vsm2.14:5.2:
Consciousness is like the villager seeing the coin, because it apprehends the mode of the object as blue,
etc., and because it extends further, reaching the penetration of its characteristics.
vsm2.14:5.3:
Understanding is like the money-changer seeing the coin, because, after apprehending the mode of the object as blue,
etc., and extending to the penetration of the characteristics, it extends still further, reaching the manifestation of the path.
vsm2.14:5.4:
That is why this act of understanding should be understood as "knowing in a particular
mode separate from the modes of perceiving and cognizing."
vsm2.14:5.5: For that is what the words "it is understanding in the sense of act of understanding" refer to.
vsm2.14:6.1: However, it is not always to be found where perception and consciousness are.
vsm2.14:6.2: But when it is, it is not disconnected from those states.
vsm2.14:6.3:
And because it cannot be taken as disconnected thus: "This is perception, this is consciousness,
this is understanding," its difference is consequently subtle and hard to see.
vsm2.14:6.4: Hence the venerable Nāgasena said: "A difficult thing, O King, has been done by the Blessed One."
vsm2.14:6.5: "What, venerable Nāgasena, is the difficult thing that has been done by the Blessed One?"
vsm2.14:6.6:
"The difficult thing, O King, done by the Blessed One was the defining of the immaterial
states of consciousness and its concomitants, which occur with a single object, and which he declared thus:
'This is contact, this is feeling, this is perception, this is volition, this is consciousness'" (Mil 87).
vsm2.14:7.1: (iii) WHAT ARE ITS CHARACTERISTIC, FUNCTION, MANIFESTATION AND PROXIMATE CAUSE?
vsm2.14:7.2: Understanding has the characteristic of penetrating the individual essences of states.
vsm2.14:7.3: Its function is to abolish the darkness of delusion, which conceals the individual essences of states.
vsm2.14:7.5: Because of the words, "One who is concentrated knows and sees correctly" (A V 3), its proximate cause is concentration.
vsm2.14:8.1: (iv) HOW MANY KINDS OF UNDERSTANDING ARE THERE?
vsm2.14:8.2: 1. Firstly, as having the characteristic of penetrating the individual essences of states, it is of one kind.
vsm2.14:8.3: 2. As mundane and supramundane it is of two kinds.
vsm2.14:8.4: 3. Likewise as subject to cankers and free from cankers, and so on,
vsm2.14:8.5: 4. As the defining of mentality and of materiality,
vsm2.14:8.6: 5. As accompanied by joy or by equanimity,
vsm2.14:8.7: 6. As the planes of seeing and of development.
vsm2.14:8.8: 7. It is of three kinds as consisting in what is reasoned, consisting in what is learnt (heard), and consisting in development.
vsm2.14:8.9: 8. Likewise as having a limited, exalted, or measureless object,
vsm2.14:8.10: 9. As skill in improvement, detriment, and means,
vsm2.14:8.11: 10. As interpreting the internal, and so on.
vsm2.14:8.12: 11. It is of four kinds as knowledge of the four truths,
vsm2.14:9.1: 9. 1. Herein, the singlefold section is obvious in meaning.
vsm2.14:9.2: 2. As regards the twofold section, the mundane is that associated with the mundane path
vsm2.14:9.3: and the supramundane is that associated with the supramundane path.
vsm2.14:9.4: So it is of two kinds as mundane and supramundane.
vsm2.14:10.1: 3. In the second dyad, that subject to cankers is that which is the object of cankers.
vsm2.14:10.2: That free from cankers is not their object.
vsm2.14:10.3: This dyad is the same in meaning as the mundane and supramundane.
vsm2.14:10.4:
The same method applies to the dyads subject to cankers and free from cankers,
associated with cankers and dissociated from cankers (Dhs 3), and so on.
vsm2.14:10.5: So it is of two kinds as subject to cankers and free from cankers, and so on.
vsm2.14:11.1:
4. In the third dyad, when a man wants to begin insight, his understanding of the defining of the four
immaterial aggregates is understanding as defining of mentality,
vsm2.14:11.2: and his understanding of the defining of the material aggregate is understanding as defining of materiality.
vsm2.14:11.3: So it is of two kinds as the defining of mentality and of materiality.
vsm2.14:12.1:
5. In the fourth dyad, understanding belonging to two of the kinds of sense-sphere profitable consciousness, and belonging
to sixteen of the kinds of path consciousness with four of the jhānas in the fivefold method, is accompanied by joy.
vsm2.14:12.2:
Understanding belonging to two of the kinds of sense-sphere profitable consciousness, and belonging to (the remaining)
four kinds of path consciousness with the fifth jhānas is accompanied by equanimity.
vsm2.14:12.3: So it is of two kinds as accompanied by joy or by equanimity.
vsm2.14:13.1: 6. In the fifth dyad, understanding belonging to the first path is the plane of seeing.
vsm2.14:13.2: Understanding belonging to the remaining three paths is the plane of development (see XXII.127).
vsm2.14:13.3: So it is of two kinds as the planes of seeing and of development.
vsm2.14:14.1:
7. As regards the triads, understanding acquired without hearing from another is that consisting in what
is reasoned because it is produced by one's own reasoning.
vsm2.14:14.2: Understanding acquired by hearing from another is that consisting in what is heard, because it is produced by hearing.
vsm2.14:14.3:
Understanding that has reached absorption, having been somehow produced by (meditative)
development, is that consisting in development.
vsm2.14:14.5: Herein, what is understanding consisting in what is reasoned?
vsm2.14:14.6:
In the spheres of work invented by ingenuity, or in the spheres of craft invented by ingenuity, or in the sorts of science
invented by ingenuity, any preference, view, choice, opinion, judgment, liking for pondering over things,
that concerns ownership of deeds (kamma) or is in conformity with truth or is of such kind as to conform with (the axioms)
'Materiality is impermanent' or 'Feeling … perception … formations … consciousness is impermanent'
vsm2.14:14.7:
that one acquires without hearing it from another—that is called understanding consisting in what is reasoned. (In the spheres)
that one acquires by hearing it from another—that is called understanding consisting in what is learnt (heard).
vsm2.14:14.8: And all understanding in anyone who has attained (an attainment) is understanding consisting in development (Vibh 324–25).
vsm2.14:14.9: So it is of three kinds as consisting in what is thought out, in what is heard, and in development.
vsm2.14:15.1: 8. In the second triad, the understanding that occurs contingent upon sense-sphere states has a limited object.
vsm2.14:15.2: That which occurs contingent upon fine-material-sphere states or immaterial-sphere states has an exalted object.
vsm2.14:15.4: That which occurs contingent upon Nibbāna has a measureless object.
vsm2.14:15.6: So it is of three kinds as having a limited, an exalted, or a measureless object.
vsm2.14:16.1: 9. In the third triad, it is increase that is called improvement.
vsm2.14:16.2: That is twofold as the elimination of harm and the arousing of good.
vsm2.14:16.3: Skill in improvement is skill in these, according as it is said:
vsm2.14:16.4: Herein, what is skill in improvement?
vsm2.14:16.5:
When a man brings these things to mind both unarisen unprofitable things do
not arise and arisen unprofitable things are abandoned in him;
vsm2.14:16.6: or when he brings these things to mind both unarisen profitable things arise
vsm2.14:16.7: and arisen profitable things advance to growth, increase, development, and perfection in him.
vsm2.14:16.8:
Whatever here is understanding, act of understanding for words elided see Dhs 16 non-delusion,
investigation of states, right view, is called skill in improvement (Vibh 325–26).
vsm2.14:17.1: Non-increase is what is called detriment.
vsm2.14:17.2: That also is twofold as the diminution of good and the arousing of harm.
vsm2.14:17.3: Skill in detriment is skill in these, according as it is said:
vsm2.14:17.4:
"Herein, what is skill in detriment? When a man brings these things to mind,
both unarisen profitable things do not arise …" (Vibh 326), and so on.
vsm2.14:18.1:
But in either of these cases any skill in means to cause the production of such and such things,
which skill occurs at that moment and is aroused on that occasion, is what is called skill in means,
vsm2.14:18.2: according as it is said: "And all understanding of means thereto is skill in means" (Vibh 326).
vsm2.14:18.3: So it is of three kinds as skill in improvement, in detriment, and in means.
vsm2.14:19.1: 10. In the fourth triad, insight-understanding initiated by apprehending one's own aggregates is interpreting the internal.
vsm2.14:19.2:
That initiated by apprehending another's aggregates or external materiality not bound
up with the faculties, that is, inanimate matter, is interpreting the external.
vsm2.14:19.3: That initiated by apprehending both is interpreting the internal and external.
vsm2.14:19.4: So it is of three kinds as interpreting the internal, and so on.
vsm2.14:20.1:
11. As regards the tetrads, in the first tetrad, knowledge that occurs
contingent upon the truth of suffering is knowledge of suffering;
vsm2.14:20.2: knowledge that occurs contingent upon the origin of suffering is knowledge of the origin of suffering;
vsm2.14:20.3: knowledge that occurs contingent upon the cessation of suffering is knowledge of the cessation of suffering;
vsm2.14:20.4:
and knowledge that occurs contingent upon the way leading to the cessation of suffering
is knowledge of the way leading to the cessation of suffering.
vsm2.14:20.5: So it is of four kinds as knowledge of the four truths.
vsm2.14:21.1:
12. In the second tetrad, the four kinds of knowledge classed as that concerned with meaning,
etc., are called the four discriminations.
vsm2.14:21.2: For this is said: "Knowledge about meaning is the discrimination of meaning (attha-paṭisambhidā).
vsm2.14:21.3: Knowledge about law is the discrimination of law (dhamma-paṭisambhidā).
vsm2.14:21.4: Knowledge about enunciation of language dealing with meaning and law is the discrimination of language (nirutti-paṭisambhidā).
vsm2.14:21.5: Knowledge about kinds of knowledge is discrimination of perspicuity (paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā)" (Vibh 293).
vsm2.14:22.1: Herein, meaning (attha) is briefly a term for the fruit of a cause (hetu).
vsm2.14:22.2: For in accordance with the cause it is served arrived at, reached, therefore it is called "meaning" (or "purpose").
vsm2.14:22.3:
But in particular the five things, namely, (i) anything conditionally produced, (ii) Nibbāna, (iii) the meaning of what
is spoken, (iv) (kamma-) result, and (v) functional (consciousness), should be understood as meaning.
vsm2.14:22.4:
When anyone reviews that meaning, any knowledge of his, falling within the category
(pabheda) concerned with meaning, is the discrimination of meaning.
vsm2.14:23.1: Law (dhamma) is briefly a term for a condition (paccaya).
vsm2.14:23.2:
For since a condition necessitates (dahati) whatever it may be, makes it occur or allows
it to happen, it is therefore called "law" (dhamma).
vsm2.14:23.3:
But in particular the five things, namely, (i) any cause that produces fruit, (ii) the noble path,
(iii) what is spoken, (iv) what is profitable, and (v) what is unprofitable, should be understood as law.
vsm2.14:23.4: When anyone reviews that law, any knowledge of his, falling within the category concerned with law, is the discrimination of law.
vsm2.14:24.1: This same meaning is shown in the Abhidhamma by the following analysis:
vsm2.14:24.2: (a) "Knowledge about suffering is the discrimination of meaning.
vsm2.14:24.3:
Knowledge about the origin of suffering is the discrimination of law. Knowledge about the cessation of suffering
is the discrimination of meaning. Knowledge about the way leading to the cessation of suffering is the discrimination of law …
vsm2.14:24.4: (b) "Knowledge about cause is the discrimination of law.
vsm2.14:24.5: Knowledge about the fruit of a cause is the discrimination of meaning …
vsm2.14:24.6: (c) "Knowledge about whatever things are born, become, brought to birth, produced, completed, made manifest,
vsm2.14:24.8: Knowledge about the things from which those things were born, became, were brought to birth, produced, completed, made manifest,
vsm2.14:24.10: (d) "Knowledge about ageing and death is the discrimination of meaning.
vsm2.14:24.11:
Knowledge about the origin of ageing and death is the discrimination of law. Knowledge about the cessation of ageing and death
is the discrimination of meaning. Knowledge about the way leading to the cessation of ageing and death
is the discrimination of law. Knowledge about birth … becoming … clinging … craving … feeling … contact … the sixfold
base … mentality-materiality … consciousness … knowledge about formations is the discrimination of meaning.
Knowledge about the origin of formations is the discrimination of law.
vsm2.14:24.12: Knowledge about the cessation of formations is the discrimination of meaning.
vsm2.14:24.13: Knowledge about the way leading to the cessation of formations is the discrimination of law …
vsm2.14:24.14:
(e) "Here a bhikkhu knows the Dhamma (Law)—the Discourses, Songs, Expositions, Stanzas,
Exclamations, Sayings, Birth Stories, Marvels, and Answers to Questions—
vsm2.14:24.15: this is called the discrimination of law.
vsm2.14:24.16:
He knows the meaning of whatever is said thus: 'This is the meaning of this that was said;
this is the meaning of this that was said'—
vsm2.14:24.17: this is called the discrimination of meaning …
vsm2.14:24.19:
On an occasion when profitable consciousness of the sense sphere has arisen that is accompanied by joy and associated
with knowledge, having a visible datum as its object … or a mental datum as its object, or contingent upon whatever it may
be, on that occasion there is contact … (for elision see Dhs §1) … there is non-wavering— these things are profitable.
vsm2.14:24.20: Knowledge about these things is the discrimination of law.
vsm2.14:24.21: Knowledge about their result is the discrimination of meaning" … (Vibh 293–95).
